sub_topics: Assuming his SC seat on Aug 20, Justice Francis H. Jardeleza aptly declared: 'I will dispense my duties with competence, integrity, probity and independence, always bearing in mind the interest of the Filipino people'
To these four traits required by Constitution (which CJP code-named 'CIPI'), may add industry to speed up cases in Court
CJP agrees that justices should promote interest of our people by, in humble view, safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity
History will judge judges on how they adhered to CIPI++
Justices often disappoint presidents who appointed them and who expected their unswerving loyalty
Because they inevitably become independent after undergoing a life-changing transformation
How? Let me begin by saying no university on earth teaches a course on how to be a SC justice
As Anthony Lewis wrote in 'Gideon's Trumpet' (1996, p. 217): 'a justice brings to the task only his character, his intellect, his education, his experience, his human understanding, his imagination'
Thereafter, CJP believes, he/she relies on creativity, innovation, reflection and prayers
Career jurists who ascended Court via judicial hierarchy are lucky in that their adjustments to lonely perches were not sudden or unexpected
Unlike those picked straight from private practice or from academe or from nonjudicial branches of government
But even career magistrates tell CJP that something does happen when they don robes of SC
All at once, new appointees feel new beginning
Immediately, they realize god-like finality of their acts and decisions which, whether right or wrong, are not reviewed, modified or reversed by any agency of the government
Instead, they are immortalized in books to be criticized, damned or acclaimed years after they have passed to the Great Beyond
Members of Congress are called upon by their constituents to account for their actions while Cabinet members must, day-by-day, merit the trust and confidence of the President
Hence, to the elected, popular approval is the powerful barometer of their success or failure
On the other hand, magistrates must live in a world of reason where logic, evidence and conscience are their only yardsticks
Permanency of tenure and independence accorded to justices by Constitution partly explain why they are able to withstand temporary political passions and rages
Their freedom to decide enables them to do things which others may think to be correct but have no courage to fulfill because of fear of electoral rejection or presidential rebuff
It is also these rare luxuries of tenure and independence that excise jurists from parochial prejudices, and help them to decide objectively and consistently
Indeed, search for principles and doctrines is the bedrock of the work of jurists
A litigation is won not because one side gets more votes from the people, but because it is upheld by the law through the process of reasoning

In SC, cases are won or lost not because of popular palatability or compromise or friendship or bargaining or pecuniary considerations, but because of reasoned arguments based on legal principles and precedents
Not to say that Court is averse to public opinion
In fact, CJP daresays that Court is effective only as long as it retains the faith and trust of the public, without which Court becomes useless
Cannot enforce its own pronouncements -- does not command army or police or 'raging mob'; neither does it have money to grease political patronage
There is a difference between shifting winds of public emotion and long-term public trust in the institution
While critics may rant from time to time against some decisions or opinions, Court must enjoy enough residual respect, with constant hope that one day it will prove to be right
Even if they may disagree, level-headed critics should respect it enough to concede its good faith, and likewise the wisdom, probity and diligence with which its members do their work
They must realize that, in our system of government, Court's function is not to mirror popular ideas but to teach and to open new vistas to enlightened opinion
In this light, mettle of magistrates is tested by their capacity to stand by their convictions when the mob rages against them, threatens their families, and chants slogans of hate
For that is the nature of our conscience -- prevents us from doing the wrong thing just because it is easy and pleasurable; rather, impels us to do what is right, no matter how painful and difficult

Such is the role of jurists -- to uphold the basic norms of society and to defend the people's constitutional rights, notwithstanding tyrants, lynch mobs and even the best intentioned but ill-informed critics
They do not lust for the brute power of the executive or the patronage of the legislature
They pray only for courage, integrity and sagacity for these are their only tools to earn the people's trust
Finally, presidents should be proud, not disappointed, when their appointees fulfill their duty with CIPI++
To win cases, they should not rely on blind loyalty; instead, they should learn how the Court functions, and how and why justices transform

stances.claim: Career jurists who ascended via the judicial hierarchy are lucky -- their adjustments to the lonely perches were not sudden or unexpected, unlike those picked straight from private practice, academe, or non-judicial branches of government; but even career magistrates tell CJ that something does happen when they don the SC robes -- all at once, new appointees feel a new beginning, immediately realizing the god-like finality of their acts and decisions which, whether right or wrong, are not reviewed, modified or reversed by any agency of the government; instead, they are immortalized in books to be criticized, damned or acclaimed years after they have passed to the Great Beyond

Members of Congress are called by constituents to account; Cabinet members day-by-day merit the President's trust -- hence to the elected, popular approval is the powerful barometer; on the other hand, magistrates must live in a world of reason where logic, evidence and conscience are their only yardsticks; permanency of tenure and independence partly explain why they withstand temporary political passions and rages, doing things others think correct but have no courage to fulfill because of fear of electoral rejection or presidential rebuff

The search for principles and doctrines is the bedrock of the work of jurists -- a litigation is won not because one side gets more votes from the people, but because it is upheld by the law through the process of reasoning; in the SC, cases are won or lost not because of popular palatability or compromise or friendship or bargaining or pecuniary considerations, but because of reasoned arguments based on legal principles and precedents

This is not to say the Court is averse to public opinion -- CJ daresays the Court is effective only as long as it retains the faith and trust of the public, without which the Court becomes useless because it cannot enforce its own pronouncements: it does not command the army or the police or the 'raging mob,' neither does it have money to grease political patronage; there is a difference between the shifting winds of public emotion and the long-term public trust in the institution; while critics may rant from time to time, the Court must enjoy enough residual respect with the constant hope that one day it will prove to be right

The mettle of magistrates is tested by their capacity to stand by their convictions when the mob rages against them, threatens their families, and chants slogans of hate -- that is the nature of our conscience: it prevents us from doing the wrong thing just because it is easy and pleasurable; rather, it impels us to do what is right, no matter how painful and difficult; such is the role of jurists -- to uphold the basic norms of society and to defend the people's constitutional rights, notwithstanding tyrants, lynch mobs and even the best-intentioned but ill-informed critics; they do not lust for the brute power of the executive or the patronage of the legislature; they pray only for courage, integrity and sagacity

Finally, presidents should be proud, not disappointed, when their appointees fulfill their duty with CIPI++ -- to win cases, they should not rely on blind loyalty; instead, they should learn how the Court functions, and how and why justices transform

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers the middle installment of his three-branch DAP-aftermath trilogy (August 24, 2014; between A403 Aug 17 'Weakened presidency' and A401 Aug 31 'Fortified legislature'). Assuming his SC seat on Aug 20, Justice Francis H. Jardeleza aptly declared, 'I will dispense my duties with competence, integrity, probity and independence, always bearing in mind the interest of the Filipino people.' To these four traits required by the Constitution (which CJ code-named 'CIPI'), may CJ add industry to speed up the cases in the Court. CJ agrees with him that justices should promote the interest of our people by, in CJ's humble view, safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity. History will judge judges on how they adhered to CIPI++. Immortalized in books: justices often disappoint the presidents who appointed them and who expected their unswerving loyalty because they inevitably become independent after undergoing a life-changing transformation. How? Let CJ begin by saying that no university on earth teaches a course on how to be a Supreme Court justice. As Anthony Lewis wrote in 'Gideon's Trumpet' (1996, p. 217), 'a justice brings to the task only his character, his intellect, his education, his experience, his human understanding, his imagination.' Thereafter, CJ believes, he/she relies on creativity, innovation, reflection and prayers. Career jurists who ascended to the Court via the judicial hierarchy are lucky in that their adjustments to the lonely perches on the highest tribunal were not sudden or unexpected, unlike those of us who were picked straight from private practice or from the academe or from the non-judicial branches of government. But even career magistrates tell CJ that something does happen when they don the robes of the SC -- all at once, new appointees feel a new beginning; immediately, they realize the god-like finality of their acts and decisions which, whether right or wrong, are not reviewed, modified or reversed by any agency of the government; instead, they are immortalized in books to be criticized, damned or acclaimed years after they have passed to the Great Beyond. Standards for decisions: members of Congress are called upon by their constituents to account for their actions while Cabinet members must day-by-day merit the trust and confidence of the President; hence, to the elected, popular approval is the powerful barometer of their success or failure. On the other hand, magistrates must live in a world of reason where logic, evidence and conscience are their only yardsticks. The permanency of tenure and the independence accorded to justices by our Constitution partly explain why they are able to withstand temporary political passions and rages -- their freedom to decide enables them to do things which others may think to be correct but have no courage to fulfill because of fear of electoral rejection or presidential rebuff; it is also these rare luxuries of tenure and independence that excise jurists from parochial prejudices and help them decide objectively and consistently. Indeed, the search for principles and doctrines is the bedrock of the work of jurists. A litigation is won not because one side gets more votes from the people, but because it is upheld by the law through the process of reasoning. In the SC, cases are won or lost not because of popular palatability or compromise or friendship or bargaining or pecuniary considerations, but because of reasoned arguments based on legal principles and precedents. This is not to say the Court is averse to public opinion -- in fact, CJ daresays the Court is effective only as long as it retains the faith and trust of the public, without which the Court becomes useless because it cannot enforce its own pronouncements: it does not command the army or the police or the 'raging mob,' neither does it have the money to grease political patronage. Public trust: there is a difference between the shifting winds of public emotion and the long-term public trust in the institution. While critics may rant from time to time against some decisions or opinions, the Court must enjoy enough residual respect, with the constant hope that one day it will prove to be right. And even if they may disagree, its level-headed critics should respect it enough to concede its good faith, and likewise the wisdom, probity and diligence with which its members do their work; they must realize that, in our system of government, the Court's function is not to mirror popular ideas but to teach and to open new vistas to enlightened opinion. In this light, the mettle of magistrates is tested by their capacity to stand by their convictions when the mob rages against them, threatens their families, and chants slogans of hate -- that is the nature of our conscience: it prevents us from doing the wrong thing just because it is easy and pleasurable; rather, it impels us to do what is right, no matter how painful and difficult. Such is the role of jurists -- to uphold the basic norms of society and to defend the people's constitutional rights, notwithstanding tyrants, lynch mobs and even the best-intentioned but ill-informed critics. They do not lust for the brute power of the executive or the patronage of the legislature; they pray only for courage, integrity and sagacity for these are their only tools to earn the people's trust. Finally, presidents should be proud, not disappointed, when their appointees fulfill their duty with CIPI++. To win cases, they should not rely on blind loyalty; instead, they should learn how the Court functions, and how and why justices transform.
